resources.string: The console\'s built-in storage chip: details and backups
This console has no built-in eMMC that andr36oid can switch on.
The built-in eMMC is switched off. Switch on Kernel Tweaks > Built-in eMMC storage, then restart the console.
The eMMC\'s details couldn\'t be read.
Switched on, but no eMMC answered. This console may not have one, or the kernel left it off because something else uses its pins. A problem report has the details.
Worn out: past its rated life
Spare blocks almost gone: back it up soon
Takes about 16 seconds and only reads
The speed test couldn\'t read the eMMC.
Copies the eMMC, or a part of it, to image files in the folder \"eMMC backup\" on the storage you pick. The eMMC is only read: the system on it stays as it is.
%1$s: all partitions, the partition table and the boot areas, to put it back exactly as it is
%1$s go to the folder \"eMMC backup\" on %2$s. The console stays awake until it\'s done.
That storage uses FAT32, which takes files up to 4 GB, so the image is split into numbered pieces (.001, .002…). Join them on a computer before using the image.
%1$s needs %2$s free for this, it has %3$s.
What was copied so far stays in the folder, but it\'s not a complete image.
Stopped. %2$s on %1$s holds an incomplete copy.
The eMMC couldn\'t be read to the end. %2$s on %1$s holds an incomplete copy.
Put andr36oid on the built-in eMMC, so the console starts without the SD card
andr36oid only installs onto the eMMC when it runs from the SD card.
andr36oid is running from the built-in eMMC. To change the installation or put the stock system back, start from the andr36oid SD card.
The test worked: andr36oid started from the eMMC.\n\nRestart now. The console starts from the SD card again, where the installation finishes. Leave the SD card in.
Step 0: Back up the stock eMMC
Step 1: Prove the SD card\'s loader
Step 2: Prove andr36oid on the eMMC
Step 3: Put the loader on the eMMC
The installer couldn\'t look at the console.
No built-in eMMC found. Switch it on in Kernel Tweaks > Built-in eMMC storage and restart.
Big enough for andr36oid (8 GB or more)
The stock system will be gone

Everything on the built-in eMMC is replaced: the system the console came with, its games and its settings. A full copy is made first and you can put it back from here, but only with this SD card and only while the console still starts.

Writing the loader that starts the console is the most dangerous thing you can do to it. If it goes wrong, the console may not switch on at all, and nothing andr36oid can do will help.\n\nConsoles whose eMMC and memory are one chip (eMCP) are the worst: they have no easy way to force them into recovery. Getting them back can mean opening the case and soldering, or may not be possible.

This is experimental. Nobody can promise it works on your console, and nobody can fix it for you if it doesn\'t.\n\nThe partition sizes are fixed now. Later andr36oid versions can only be put on the eMMC if they fit.
How the eMMC is split up
system and vendor get room to grow for later versions, your apps and data get the rest.
All %1$s of the eMMC (sectors 0-%2$d) and its two boot areas are read, read again to compare, copied to %3$s, and read back. Nothing is written to the eMMC.
eMMC sectors 64-32767 (the stock loader, 16 MiB) are blanked. Then you restart: the console has to start from the SD card\'s loader on its own.

A new partition table (eMMC sectors 0-33 and %1$d-%2$d); BOOT, system and vendor copied from the SD card; the start of metadata, misc, cache and userdata blanked:\n%3$sThen andr36oid starts from the eMMC once, as a test.
The SD card\'s sectors 64-32767 (its loader) are copied to the eMMC, after one more warning.

Every write is read back and compared. If anything doesn\'t match, the installer stops and writes nothing more. Steps 1 and 2 are each proven by a restart before the next one. Step 3 is the only write that can\'t be tried out first.
The stock eMMC is backed up. Next is step 1: its loader is blanked, then you restart.
Step 1 passed: the console started from the SD card\'s loader on its own.\n\nNext is step 2: andr36oid is copied to the eMMC (a few minutes), then it starts from there once.
Step 2 passed: andr36oid started from the eMMC.\n\nNext is step 3: the loader goes onto the eMMC.

The eMMC\'s loader is blank. Restart now: the console has to start from the SD card\'s loader on its own, and this page opens again.\n\nIf it doesn\'t come back: hold power for 7 seconds and switch it on again. If it still doesn\'t start, this console needs its stock loader. The backup is in %1$s on this SD card.

andr36oid is on the eMMC. Restart now: it starts from the eMMC once, as a test. Its first start sets things up and takes a few minutes. When it says the test worked, restart again.\n\nIf it hangs: hold power for 7 seconds and switch it on again. It then starts from the SD card as usual, and this page says what happened.

Shut the console down, take the SD card out once it is off, then switch it on: andr36oid now starts from the eMMC.\n\nWith a different bootable SD card in, the console starts from the card, as before.
Don\'t press anything while it starts from the eMMC. Wait until this wizard comes back up at step 2.
Make the data card start again?

andr36oid on the eMMC kept Android\'s data on an SD card, and that card can\'t start the console by itself. It can become a normal andr36oid SD card again: your apps, saves and settings stay on it.\n\nIf it isn\'t the card in the console now, put it in slot 2 first.
This SD card starts andr36oid as before, with your apps and data. Shut the console down. Without the card, it starts the stock system.
The card in slot 2 starts andr36oid now, with your apps and data. Shut the console down and put that card in slot 1 instead of this one. Without an SD card, the console starts the stock system.
Shut the console down, take the SD card out once it is off, then switch it on to use the stock system.

This writes the loader that starts the console onto the eMMC. Everything before this was tested. This is not: the loader has to read U-Boot from the eMMC, which the stock loader shows works on this board, but these exact bytes never ran from the eMMC.\n\nIf it fails, the console doesn\'t switch on any more, with or without an SD card.
It\'s my fault if this goes wrong
Hold A for 10 seconds. Letting go starts over.
The installer has no loader checksum from step 1.
andr36oid is installed on the eMMC. Without an SD card the console starts from the eMMC; with a different bootable SD card in, it starts from the card.
Nothing more was written after this. Your stock eMMC is backed up in %1$s.\n\nPut the stock eMMC back, or leave it as it is?
Nothing was written to the eMMC.
%1$s was cut off before it finished (power lost?).
andr36oid didn\'t start from the eMMC in the test.
The installer stopped without saying how it went.

Copies this SD card\'s andr36oid to the eMMC: its BOOT files, system and vendor, and U-Boot if it changed. Apps, data and settings on the eMMC stay.\n\nKeep the console charging. If the update is cut off, the console starts from the SD card until you run it again.
Everything andr36oid wrote to the eMMC is replaced by the backup in %1$s. The backup is checked first, and the eMMC is compared with it afterwards. This takes a few minutes.
Step 0 only reads the eMMC. Nothing is written to it yet.
Write the loader to the eMMC

Installing on the eMMC takes a while: everything written is read back and compared with the original before the wizard moves on. That\'s deliberate. One bad write in the wrong place can leave the console unable to start at all, so each step has to be proven correct before the next one begins.
The backup is written back to the eMMC part by part. Then the whole eMMC is read back and compared with the backup, so you know it is exactly the stock eMMC again.
The new andr36oid is copied from the SD card to the eMMC one part at a time. Each part is read back and compared with the SD card before the next one starts.
andr36oid is already on the eMMC

andr36oid was installed on this console\'s eMMC from another SD card, so this card has no records of it.\n\nThis card can take it over, without writing anything to the eMMC. Then you can update the eMMC to this card\'s andr36oid, or put the stock system back.
The stock eMMC\'s backup is on this card: %1$s
This card has no backup of the stock eMMC. To put the stock system back later, copy its folder from the other card\'s EASYROMS (in \"eMMC backup\") to this card\'s EASYROMS first.
The eMMC holds the stock system again, checked against the backup. andr36oid runs from this SD card, and nothing more needs to be done.\n\nWithout the SD card, the console starts the stock system.
Keep the console switched on and the SD card in until this is done.
andr36oid is on the eMMC, but its test start hasn\'t run yet. Test now: the console restarts and starts from the eMMC once.
The last update of andr36oid on the eMMC didn\'t finish. The eMMC may not start until the update runs again. The SD card still starts the console.
Putting the stock eMMC back didn\'t finish. The eMMC is part stock, part andr36oid and may not start. Run it again to finish it.
Stock eMMC back, but not exactly

Everything andr36oid wrote is back as it was in the backup and checked. The boot areas differ, though, and andr36oid never writes them. Shut the console down, take the SD card out once it is off, then switch it on to see if the stock system starts.

This writes an SD card image of your choice to the eMMC, in place of the stock system. It is not andr36oid, and nothing here is tested.

The image's own loader replaces the console's. If it doesn't suit this console, the console may never start again, not even from an SD card. If the eMMC is soldered on (eMCP), only soldering work can bring it back.

A backup of the stock eMMC is made first, if there isn't one yet. andr36oid can put it back only while the console still starts from an SD card.
Images (.img, .img.gz, .img.xz, or .zip with one .img) in internal storage, in Download and on the SD card\'s BOOT partition.
No images found. Copy one to internal storage or to Download, then look again.
%1$s: %2$s. The eMMC: %3$s. A packed image is bigger once unpacked; it is checked before anything is written.\n\nEverything on the eMMC is replaced by this image.
This image is bigger than the eMMC, so it can\'t be written.
The image is read once to check it, written to the eMMC, then read back from it.
%1$s is on the eMMC and reads back the same. Shut the console down, take the SD card out once it is off, then switch it on.
Your own image is on the eMMC
%1$s (%2$s) was written to the eMMC in the advanced mode. It is not andr36oid. You can install andr36oid, put the stock system back, or write another image.
Writing an image to the eMMC didn\'t finish. The eMMC holds only part of it and won\'t start. Write an image again, or put the stock system back.
Where should Android keep its data?

Android\'s data is your apps, their saves and settings, and your files. It can stay on an SD card instead of the eMMC, which helps when the eMMC is small. A data card has to stay in the console: without it, Android doesn\'t start.\n\nYou choose now. The data card is made last, after the eMMC test start worked.
Like any installation. The SD card can come out at the end.
Its data (%1$s) stays where it is: the eMMC continues where the SD card left off. The card then can\'t start the console by itself and has to stay in.
On a new card in slot 2
The %1$s card in slot 2 is erased and gets Android\'s data. This SD card stays as it is.
Put a card in slot 2 and open this page again to choose this.
What goes on the new card?

Everything on the card in slot 2 (%1$s, %2$s) is erased.\n\nIt gets this SD card\'s layout, Android\'s data as you choose, and EASYROMS for your games. It can\'t start the console by itself: the console starts from the eMMC and uses the card for its data.
Android\'s data with every installed app, and EASYROMS (%1$s). Needs %2$s.
Installed apps and their data come along. EASYROMS starts empty. Needs %1$s.
Android starts as new and EASYROMS is empty. Installed apps are not transferred. Needs %1$s.
Too small: needs %1$s, the card has %2$s.
Also copy the apps that came with andr36oid (AUTOAPK, %1$s)
Without that copy, the apps that came with andr36oid stay only on this SD card, and only as long as its AUTOAPK partition is there.
The apps that came with andr36oid aren\'t on this SD card any more (AUTOAPK goes once they are installed). They can\'t come along to a fresh start.
Make this SD card the data card

The eMMC gets a note to use this card's data. Then this card stops starting the console: its start files are renamed and its loader is blanked. Its system partitions are blanked at the first start from the eMMC.

Afterwards, shut down and switch on with the card left in: andr36oid starts from the eMMC and keeps its data on this card.

The andr36oid SD card flasher can make the card start the console again. It then offers to update the eMMC and make the card a data card again.

The card in slot 2 is erased and made a data card. Android\'s data is copied to it at one start from the eMMC, where the data isn\'t in use: the console restarts, copies, and comes back to this SD card to finish. Leave both cards in.
The card in slot 2 is erased and made a data card. Android starts fresh on it.
If the copy at the start from the eMMC finished, the eMMC now gets the note to use the new card\'s data. If it didn\'t, copy again.
The new card is made. Finishing tells the eMMC to use it.
Restart now. The console starts from the eMMC once and copies Android\'s data to the new card there. This can take a while. Then it starts from this SD card again to finish.
Shut the console down and switch it on again with this card left in: andr36oid starts from the eMMC and keeps its data on the card. Without the card, Android doesn\'t start.

Shut the console down and take this SD card out of slot 1. Leave the new card in (either slot): andr36oid then starts from the eMMC and keeps its data on the new card.\n\nThis SD card is unchanged. In slot 1 it still starts the console, as before.
andr36oid started from the eMMC. Android\'s data is now copied from the SD card to the new card, while neither of them is in use. Keep the console on.
Copied. Restart now: the console starts from the SD card once more to finish the data card. Leave both cards in.
The card and Android\'s data are being prepared. This can take a while.
Update the eMMC to this version and make this card a data card again?

This card is the data card of andr36oid on the eMMC. The andr36oid SD card flasher updated it, so the console started from the card.

Update eMMC copies this card's andr36oid to the eMMC (apps and data stay) and makes the card a data card again. The console then starts from the eMMC.

Keep it an SD card: the card stays as it is and this isn't asked again.
The eMMC is updated and this card is a data card again. Restart now: andr36oid starts from the eMMC.
Go back to the stock system

The stock system can only be put back on the eMMC while the console runs from an SD card, and your data card can't start the console by itself. So it takes two steps:

1. Make the card start: the data card gets this andr36oid and a loader, so it starts the console by itself. Your apps, saves and settings stay on it.

2. Start from the card. eMMC Installation then offers to put the stock system back from its backup.
The data card starts by itself now
Shut the console down, then switch it on: it starts from the data card. eMMC Installation then opens and offers to put the stock system back.

Shut the console down. Take the card out of slot 1 if there is one, move the data card from slot 2 to slot 1, then switch the console on: it starts from the data card. eMMC Installation then opens and offers to put the stock system back.
Put the stock system back on the eMMC?

You asked to go back to the stock system. This card started the console, with your apps and data.

Put the stock eMMC back writes its backup in %1$s to the eMMC. Afterwards the console starts the stock system without an SD card, and andr36oid with this card in slot 1.

Keep andr36oid on the eMMC brings the eMMC up to this card instead, and makes the card a data card again.

No backup of this console\'s stock eMMC was found. Copy its folder (in \"eMMC backup\") to this card\'s EASYROMS, then open eMMC Installation again.\n\nKeep andr36oid on the eMMC brings the eMMC up to this card instead, and makes the card a data card again.
Shut the console down. Without an SD card it starts the stock system. With this card in slot 1 it starts andr36oid, with your apps and data.
Keep this card a normal SD card?

The andr36oid on the eMMC would then be a different system from the one your data on this card is set up for. That may work if you time when the card goes in, but it isn't recommended or supported.

For two Android installs, use a second SD card with the full andr36oid image instead.

Keep it an SD card anyway?
This card stays an SD card
It starts andr36oid as before, and eMMC Installation won\'t ask again. The eMMC isn\'t changed.
